summary.title: How to Build Good Software
summary.one_liner: Good software comes from solving a clearly defined problem with simple scope, reused code, iterative testing, and strong engineers, rather than from budget or feature count.
takeaways: Bad software usually stems from project management: unclear problem definitions, large requirement lists, and handing off to external teams that take the knowledge with them.
Reuse existing open source code and cloud services to build faster, and focus effort on novel problems.
Software is limited by complexity, so alternate between adding features and simplifying the codebase, and prioritise requirements into critical, high-value and nice-to-have tiers.
Validate the real problem early by talking to users, use cheap disposable prototypes, then roll out to small groups before larger audiences.
Small teams of strong engineers can outperform large average teams; keep knowledge in-house alongside external help.
summary.summary: Li Hongyi, writing in ETHOS Issue 21 (July 2019), argues that bad software is mainly a project management problem rather than a funding or technology problem. He describes how large, requirement-driven projects built by external vendors lose the knowledge needed to maintain them. The essay builds on three observations: reuse makes good software quick to build, complexity rather than resources limits what software can do, and the main value lies in accumulated knowledge. It closes with three principles (start simple, seek out problems and iterate, hire the best engineers), supported by examples from Singapore government apps such as Parking.sg, Form.gov.sg and Data.gov.sg.
